description: We’re a multidisciplinary team curious about space and planetary science. Our interests span astrophysics, space exploration, satellites, AI, data visualization, graphic design, and storytelling. We work with NASA’s open data and turn it into practical solutions, and we try to explain complex space science so that anyone curious about it can follow along.
summary: Mission Architect is a browser game that lets students design and fly a space mission under real constraints. Players choose a mission objective, orbit, launch vehicle, power system, communications link, and scientific instruments, while a live dashboard tracks budget, mass, power, and data downlink. Their design is then flown through ten simulated years, where radiation upsets and component failures test whether it has enough margin. Each run ends with a science return score and design lessons that explain what to fix. The sun-synchronous orbit uses NASA’s Landsat 8 values (705 km altitude and 185 km swath), and the instrument names are inspired by Landsat 8’s OLI and TIRS sensors. Other numbers are illustrative teaching values. Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it helps students see how trade-offs shape a mission from concept to operation.
details:
Mission Architect is a browser game that teaches students how a space mission comes together. Players work through six decisions: mission objective, orbit, launch vehicle, power system, communications, and scientific instruments. A live dashboard tracks budget, mass, power, and data downlink, and blocks launch when a design doesn’t fit. The mission then flies through ten simulated years, where radiation upsets, component faults, and power degradation test whether the design has enough margin. Each run ends with a science return score and design lessons that explain what to fix before the next flight.

How it works: Each choice changes the mission’s numbers immediately. Hovering over an option previews its effect on the spacecraft and the dashboard, and the expected science percentage updates as players make changes. The game runs in any modern browser, with no installation, login, or data collection.

Benefits: Students get hands-on experience with engineering trade-offs that are usually abstract, such as how a larger instrument affects power, data, and budget. Teachers can use it in class, and students can replay it to try different strategies.

Intended impact: The project is meant to make space engineering more accessible to students and self-learners, and to show that good missions depend on balancing competing limits. It’s designed to spark interest in space careers and to show how NASA data can inform real design choices.

Tools and technologies: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks or build step. The orbit and satellite visuals use inline SVG animation, and the background starfield uses the HTML canvas. Typography uses Google Fonts (Orbitron and Inter). The code is hosted on GitHub, with GitHub Pages for the live version and a Codespaces configuration for development. We used Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help write and refine the code and presentation slides. No special hardware is required; any laptop, tablet, or phone can run it.

Creativity: The project turns a systems engineering problem into a game. Instead of reading about trade-offs, players feel their consequences through live feedback, a ten-year simulation with random events, and mission-control style visuals, including a holographic Earth on the cover slide.

Factors considered:

  • NASA data: The sun-synchronous orbit uses real values from NASA’s Landsat 8 mission (705 km altitude and 185 km swath). Instrument names are inspired by Landsat 8’s OLI and TIRS sensors.
  • Accuracy: Masses, costs, power, and science values are clearly labeled as illustrative teaching numbers, not NASA data.
  • Accessibility: The layout adapts to smaller screens, animations respect users who turn off motion, and keyboard arrow keys move between steps.
  • Cost and sustainability: The game is a static site that can be hosted for free and needs no servers.
  • Privacy: The game stores no personal data.

Limitations: The simulation is a teaching model. Its event probabilities and performance numbers are simplified and haven’t been checked by engineers. Future versions could replace more values with NASA mission data and add more missions.
